source_text:
ἀγγέλους. Hebr 3,13 Ὥσπερ μίαν ἡμέραν τὸν παρόντα αἰῶνα εἰσάγει. Hebr 4,12
Μερισμὸν ψυχῆς καὶ πνεύματος λέγει, ὅταν ἡ μὲν ψυχὴ προσπάσχει τῷ σώματι, τοῦ
δὲ ἁγίου πνεύματος ἡ χάρις ἀνθέλκει πρὸς τὰ οὐράνια. Hebr 6,1–2 Ἐπειδὴ ἡ ἀρχὴ τοῦ
Χριστοῦ ἀπὸ τοῦ Ἰουδαϊσμοῦ–κατὰ νόμον γὰρ ἐπολιτεύσατο–, διὰ τοῦτο λέγει· τοῦτ'
ἀφέντες ἐπὶ 349 τὴν τελειότητα φερώμεθα, εἰδότες ὅτι κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ
δεῖ εἶναι τοῦ ἄνευ νόμου μέλλοντος ἱερέως εἶναι. Ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων, καὶ πίστεως
ἐπὶ θεόν, βαπτισμῶν. τοῖς Χριστιανοῖς νεκρά ἐστι τὰ γήϊνα. ἄτοπον οὖν ἔστι, φησίν,
ἀποστάντας τῆς διαγωγῆς ταύτης, εἴτε τῆς κατὰ πίστιν, εἴτε ἀπὸ τοῦ νενεκρῶσθαι
τοῖς πᾶσιν, ἐλθεῖν πάλιν ἐπὶ τοὺς κατὰ νόμον βαπτισμούς. ὁ κύριος ἐλθὼν μετάνοιαν
ἐκήρυξεν, λέγων· μετανοεῖτε· ἤγγικε γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τῶν οὐρανῶν· μετάνοιαν δὲ
ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων. οὕτως οὖν ἀναγνωστέον· μετανοίας ἀπὸ νεκρῶν ἔργων, ἀντὶ
τοῦ τῆς ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν ἔργων μετανοίας. ὃ οὖν λέγει τοιοῦτόν ἐστιν· οὐ δεῖ
ἀφέντας τὴν μετάνοιαν τὴν ἀπὸ τῶν νεκρῶν ἔργων καὶ τὴν πίστιν τὴν εἰς θεὸν καὶ
τὸ βάπτισμα–ὃ πληθυντικῶς ὠνόμασεν διὰ τὸ πλῆθος τῶν καταξιουμένων. εἴρηκε δὲ
βαπτισμῶν καὶ τὴν διδαχήν, καὶ τὴν ἐπίθεσιν τῶν χειρῶν δι' ἧς αἱ χειροτονίαι, καὶ
τῆς ἀναστάσεως τὴν ἐλπίδα καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς–ἀνατρέχειν ἐπὶ τὸν νόμον. τοῦτο δὲ
προκατασκευάζει, ἐπειδὴ οἱ ἐν νόμῳ ἱερεῖς νόμον ἐξεδίκουν, ὁ δὲ Μελχισεδὲκ ἐκτὸς
ἦν νόμου· οὐ δὲ ἐλθὼν κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ ἦν. οὐ δεῖ, φησίν, ἀφέντας τὸν
κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ ἐκδικεῖν τὴν ἐν νόμῳ ἱερατείαν, ἵνα τὰ ἐν νόμῳ ᾖ
ἑστῶτα. θεμέλιον δὲ εἶπε τὰ ἐν νόμῳ, ἐπειδὴ προοίμιον εὐσεβείας γεγένηται τοῖς
ἀνθρώποις. Hebr 6,6 Νεκροὺς ἤγειραν οἱ ἀπόστολοι. αὕτη δὲ ἡ δύναμις τῆς
ἀναστάσεως ἦν. παραδειγματίζοντας εἶπεν, ὅτι εἰ μυστήριον τὸ βάπτισμα, τὸ ἅπαξ
ἀρκεῖ. ἐὰν δὲ δεύτερον γίνηται τὸ πρᾶγμα, καταφρόνησις καὶ παραδειγματισμός.
Hebr 6,7–8 Ὑπόδειγμα ἔλαβεν, οὐκ εἰς τὸ βάπτισμα–πῶς γὰρ δεύτερον βάπτισμα
ἐκώλυεν; –ἀλλὰ τὴν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος δύναμιν πολλάκις εὐεργετοῦσαν. Hebr
6,17 Ἀνωτέρω εἰπὼν τὴν πληροφορίαν τῆς ἐλπίδος ἐδήλωσεν ὅτι ὁ θεὸς παρέσχε τῷ
Ἀβραὰμ πληροφορίαν, οὐ τὴν δι' ἔργων τὴν τῇ πολιτείᾳ προσήκουσαν, ἀλλὰ τὴν δι'
οἰκονομίας. 350 Ἀδύνατον ὀμόσαντα τὸν θεὸν μετατεθῆναι, ἀδύνατον ἦν
μετατεθῆναι τὴν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας δύναμιν. Hebr 7,1–2 Οὐχ ἁπλῶς μέμνηται ὅπως
συνήντησεν ὁ Μελχισεδὲκ τῷ Ἀβραὰμ περιγεγονότι τῶν Ἀσσυρίων, καὶ ἔδωκεν
αὐτῷ δεκάτας ἀπὸ πάντων, ἀλλὰ δεικνὺς ὅτι ὁ προπάτωρ τῆς Λευϊτικῆς φυλῆς ἱερεῖ
ἐχρήσατο τῷ Μελχισεδέκ. κρείσσων ἄρα ἡ ἱερωσύνη ἡ ἄνευ νόμου τῆς ἱερωσύνης
pass_a_gloss:
[continuing the Hebrews 2:5-9 note] ... angels.
Hebrews 3:13. He brings in the present age as one day.
Hebrews 4:12. He speaks of a division of soul and spirit when the soul suffers along with the body, but the grace of the Holy Spirit pulls the other way toward heavenly things.
Hebrews 6:1-2. Since the beginning of Christ was from Judaism, for he lived as a citizen according to the law, for this reason he says: leaving this, let us be carried on to perfection, knowing that it must be according to the order of Melchizedek, (the priesthood) of the one who was to be priest without law. "From dead works, and of faith toward God, of baptisms." For Christians earthly things are dead. It is absurd, then, he says, that those who have stood away from this way of life, whether the one according to faith or the one from having been made dead to all things, should come back again to the baptisms (washings) according to the law. The Lord, having come, preached repentance, saying: "Repent, for the kingdom of the heavens has drawn near"; and repentance from dead works. So it must be read thus: "of repentance from dead works," in place of: of the repentance from the dead works. What he says, then, is this: one must not, having left the repentance from the dead works and the faith toward God and baptism (which he named in the plural because of the multitude of those deemed worthy; and he spoke of the teaching of baptisms, and the laying on of hands, through which the ordinations (happen), and the hope of resurrection and the rest), run back to the law. And this he prepares in advance, since the priests in the law were defending the law, but Melchizedek was outside law; and the one who came was according to the order of Melchizedek. One must not, he says, having left the one according to the order of Melchizedek, defend the priesthood in the law, so that the things in the law may be standing. And he called the things in the law a foundation, since it has become a prelude of piety to human beings.
Hebrews 6:6 (edition label). The apostles raised the dead. And this was the power of the resurrection. He said "making an example (a public show)," because if baptism is a mystery, the once suffices. But if the thing happens a second time, (it is) contempt and public shaming.
Hebrews 6:7-8. He took an illustration not for baptism (for how was he forbidding a second baptism?) but for the power of the Holy Spirit doing good many times.
Hebrews 6:17. Having spoken above of the full assurance of the hope, he showed that God provided Abraham full assurance, not the one through works, which belongs to the way of life, but the one through the economy (dispensation). God having sworn, it is impossible (for him) to be changed; it was impossible for the power of the promise to be changed.
Hebrews 7:1-2. Not idly does he mention how Melchizedek met Abraham, who had prevailed over the Assyrians, and he gave him tithes from all, but showing that the forefather of the Levitical tribe used Melchizedek as priest. So the priesthood without law is greater than the priesthood [continues in the next section: in the law]
pass_b_english: On Hebrews 3:13: He presents the present age as a single day.
On Hebrews 4:12: He speaks of a dividing of soul and spirit when the soul is drawn to share what the body feels, while the grace of the Holy Spirit pulls the other way, toward heavenly things.

On Hebrews 6:1–2: Christ’s beginning was in Judaism, for he lived according to the law. That is why he says: let us leave this behind and press on to perfection, knowing that the one who was to be a priest without the law had to be after the order of Melchizedek. “From dead works, and of faith toward God, of baptisms”: for Christians, earthly things are dead. So it is absurd, he says, for people who have left this way of life, whether we call it the life of faith or the life of those who have died to everything, to go back again to the washings of the law. When the Lord came, he preached repentance, saying, “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has come near” (Matthew 4:17); and that repentance is repentance from dead works. So the phrase should be read like this: “of repentance from dead works”, meaning “of the repentance that turns from dead works”. What he means, then, is this: we must not abandon repentance from dead works, faith in God and baptism and run back to the law. He named baptism in the plural because of the great number of those found worthy of it; and he spoke of the teaching about baptisms, the laying on of hands, by which ordinations are made, the hope of the resurrection and the rest. He is preparing the ground for what follows: the priests under the law upheld the law, but Melchizedek stood outside the law, and the one who came was after the order of Melchizedek. We must not, he says, abandon the priest after the order of Melchizedek and take up the cause of the priesthood under the law, as if to keep the things of the law standing. He called the things of the law a “foundation” because they were, for human beings, the prelude to godliness.

On Hebrews 6:5–6: The apostles raised the dead, and that was the power of the resurrection. He said “holding him up to contempt” because, if baptism is a mystery, once is enough. If the act is repeated, it becomes contempt and public shame.

On Hebrews 6:7–8: He took this illustration not with baptism in view (how could it be, when he was ruling out a second baptism?) but for the power of the Holy Spirit, which does us good again and again.

On Hebrews 6:17: Having spoken earlier of “the full assurance of hope” (Hebrews 6:11), he showed that God gave Abraham full assurance, not the kind that comes through works and belongs to one’s way of life, but the kind that comes through God’s own dispensation. Once God had sworn, he could not change; the power of the promise could not be altered.

On Hebrews 7:1–2: He does not mention for nothing how Melchizedek met Abraham after his victory over the Assyrians, and how Abraham gave him a tenth of everything. He means to show that the forefather of the tribe of Levi had Melchizedek for his priest. So the priesthood without the law is greater than the priesthood …

lemmas.gloss: be affected along with, be attached in feeling
hold up to contempt, public shaming (Hebrews 6:6)

choices.term: Ὥσπερ μίαν ἡμέραν τὸν παρόντα αἰῶνα εἰσάγει.
choices.english: On Hebrews 3:13: He presents the present age as a single day.
choices.why: SOURCE_ISSUES item 4 called this a broken fragment. It is a whole sentence on 'as long as it is called Today'; the old English joined it to the stray word 'Angels.'
rejected: Angels. Just as he leads in for one day the present age (old)

choices.term: οὐ δὲ ἐλθὼν κατὰ τὴν τάξιν Μελχισεδὲκ ἦν
choices.english: and the one who came was after the order of Melchizedek
choices.why: Read ὁ for οὐ (a one-letter slip in the transcription); with οὐ the clause says nothing ('and not having come according to the order, he was Melchizedek', old). Recorded in translator_notes.
rejected: and not having come according to the order, he was Melchizedek (old)

choices.term: ὃ πληθυντικῶς ὠνόμασεν … καὶ τὰ ἑξῆς
choices.english: parenthesis moved after the main clause in Pass B
choices.why: The Greek sets a long parenthesis inside 'we must not abandon … and run back to the law'; Pass B states the main clause first, then the parenthesis, inside the same paragraph. Nothing added or dropped.

The note first explains 'the powers of the age to come' (6:5: the apostles raised the dead), then 'holding him up to contempt' (6:6); labelled by its words. The old English printed '(Hebrews 6:5)' only.

choices.english: how could it be, when he was ruling out a second baptism?
choices.why: The rain that falls often (6:7) cannot stand for baptism, since 6:4–6 has just ruled out a second baptism; old English 'how could a second baptism be prevented?' reversed it.
rejected: for how could a second baptism be prevented? (old)

choices.english: Once God had sworn, he could not change
choices.why: Severian's paraphrase of 6:17–18 (the unchangeable oath); old 'It is impossible, having made God swear, to be changed' made someone else swear.

choices.english: after his victory over the Assyrians
choices.why: περιγίγνομαι + genitive = prevail over; old 'when the Assyrians were surrounding' was wrong. Severian's 'Assyrians' is kept.
